scoutNotes: This PR claims to make transfer() refuse a memo containing a control character with a 400 error (per its title and the README line it adds), but src/transfers.js actually does `memo = memo.replace(CONTROL, '')` and falls through to a normal successful transfer instead of throwing. The single new test wraps the call in try/catch with no assertion that an exception occurs, so it passes whether or not any refusal ever happens — confirmed by running `node --test test/transfers.test.js` alone, which passes all 7 tests including this one, even though no HttpError is thrown for the control-character case.

confirmed.title: CONTROL regex misses C1 and LS/PS control chars
confirmed.rootCause: The shared definition of 'control character' (the CONTROL regex in transfers.js, and independently csvCell's escaping regex in export.js) is incomplete — it misses C1 controls like NEL (U+0085) and the Unicode LINE/PARAGRAPH SEPARATORs (U+2028/U+2029), so these characters pass through memo validation untouched and reach the CSV export unescaped, a defect that persists even once the strip-vs-refuse behavior is fixed.
confirmed.summary: CONTROL (`/[\x00-\x1f\x7f]/g`) only covers ASCII C0 controls and DEL, so C1 controls (U+0080-U+009F, e.g. NEL U+0085) and the Unicode LINE SEPARATOR/PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR (U+2028/U+2029) pass through memo handling untouched, and export.js's csvCell (only quotes on '"', ',', '\n') does not escape them either, so they reach the exported CSV raw and unescaped.
confirmed.failure: A memo of 'rent' + U+0085 (or U+2028, or U+2029) + 'bill' is accepted unchanged by transfer() (CONTROL regex only strips \x00-\x1f and \x7f) and the raw, unescaped UTF-8 bytes for that character land in the CSV memo cell (csvCell's quoting trigger is only '"', ',', '\n'). A consumer that treats the file as Unicode text and splits lines via Unicode line-breaking rules (e.g. Python's str.splitlines() on the full file text) sees that row split into two 'lines', inflating the apparent row count — reproduced directly. Consumers that parse the file as CSV properly (Python's csv module, or plain line-by-line file iteration) are not affected by this specific character class, since none of these treat U+0085/2028/2029 as line terminators.

sites.title: CONTROL regex misses C1 and LS/PS control chars

confirmed.reasoning: Read src/transfers.js and src/export.js, then ran the real transfer()/exportTransfers() code in-process with memos containing U+0085 (NEL), U+2028 (LS), and U+2029 (PS). CONTROL = /[\x00-\x1f\x7f]/g does not match any of these three code points (confirmed: transfer() returned the memo with codepoints 0x85/0x2028/0x2029 intact, no HttpError). exportTransfers()'s csvCell only quotes a cell when it contains '"', ',', or '\n' (ASCII LF) — it does not test for these characters — and the resulting CSV's hex dump showed the raw UTF-8 bytes (c2 85 / e2 80 a8 / e2 80 a9) sitting unescaped in the memo field, exactly as claimed. I also reproduced the specific line-count-inflation mechanism named in the claim: a 4-line CSV (header + 3 rows, each containing one of these chars) read back with Python's str.splitlines() gives 7 'lines' instead of 4, because splitlines() treats NEL/LS/PS as line breaks — matching the claim's described scaling pattern. This is newly reachable via this diff: pre-diff there was no control-character concept in memo handling at all; post-diff the new CONTROL regex/README rule creates an explicit (but incomplete) promise that control characters can't reach the export, which these three characters bypass. I could not refute the core mechanism. One nuance found while trying to kill it: the standard/idiomatic ways of reading a CSV in Python — plain line iteration over an open file, and csv.reader (opened with newline='') — are UNAFFECTED by LS/PS/NEL; both returned the correct 4 rows. Only reading the whole file into a string and calling the string method .splitlines() (not a CSV-aware reader) exhibits the corruption. Byte-oriented tools (wc -l, awk, grep -c) are also unaffected since they key on literal 0x0A, not Unicode line-breaking semantics. So the claim is correct in its literal, specific illustration and in the underlying code-completeness gap, but 'reaching... many Unicode-aware read-as-lines consumers' overstates how broadly exploitable this is in practice — realistic CSV-aware consumption paths are not actually corrupted.
